original: Founded 1766 in London by James Christie
final_text: James Christie held his first sale in Pall Mall, London, on 5 December 1766; lot one, 'six breakfast pint basons and plates', was knocked down for 19 shillings.
source_note: Country Life: Christie's first sale, first lot, price

original: Headquarters: King Street, St. James's, London + Rockefeller Center, NYC
final_text: Christie's main salerooms are at 8 King Street, St James's, London, and 20 Rockefeller Plaza in New York's Rockefeller Center.
source_note: Christie's own locations page lists both salerooms

original: Sold: da Vinci's "Salvator Mundi" for $450.3M (2017) - record
final_text: Christie's New York sold Leonardo's Salvator Mundi on 15 November 2017 for $450.3 million with premium, the auction record; it had sold in 2005 at a small US regional sale, reportedly under $10,000.
source_note: Art Newspaper; 2005 regional sale under $10,000

original: Private sales, evening sales (the glamorous events), day sales
final_text: In 1779 James Christie valued Robert Walpole's Houghton pictures; the planned sale was cancelled when Catherine the Great bought all 204 works en bloc for £40,555 and sent a ship to fetch them.
source_note: Walpole collection sold to Catherine via Christie valuation

original: "White glove sale" = every lot sold
final_text: A 'white glove' sale means every lot sold; the May 2018 Peggy and David Rockefeller sale at Christie's New York was one, all 1,500+ lots, $832 million, proceeds to charity.
source_note: ATG: white-glove Rockefeller sale, record single-owner total

original: The paddle, the auctioneer's gavel, the tension in the room
final_text: On 11 May 2015 Jussi Pylkkanen hammered Picasso's Les Femmes d'Alger (Version O) at Christie's NY after 11.5 minutes of bidding, $179.4M; at $152M he told the room 'We're in new territory'.
source_note: Art Newspaper: bidding duration, quote, final price

original: Founded 1744 - oldest auction house
final_text: Sotheby's began on 11 March 1744, when bookseller Samuel Baker sold Sir John Stanley's library in London's Strand for £826; it is the oldest of the major international houses, not the oldest anywhere.
source_note: Sotheby's history page: first sale, Stanley library, £826

original: Headquarters: New Bond Street, London + York Avenue, NYC
final_text: Sotheby's left York Avenue: on 8 November 2025 it opened its new global HQ in Marcel Breuer's former Whitney building on Madison Avenue; over its New Bond Street door sits a c.1320 BC Sekhmet bust.
source_note: Breuer HQ opening Nov 2025; Sekhmet via heritagedaily

original: Rival to Christie's - they divide the art world
final_text: The rivals once colluded: Sotheby's chairman Alfred Taubman was convicted on 5 Dec 2001 of fixing seller commissions with Christie's, got a year and a day; the houses paid $512M in settlements.
source_note: CNN conviction; settlement figure via artnet scandals review

original: Famous sales: Gauguin's "Nafea Faa Ipoipo" - $300M (private 2015)
final_text: Sotheby's invented the gala sale on 15 Oct 1958: seven Goldschmidt pictures by Manet, Cezanne, Renoir, Van Gogh made £781,000 in 21 minutes; Cezanne's Garcon au gilet rouge hit a record £220,000.
source_note: Nafea was private, not Sotheby's; Goldschmidt sale facts

original: Online bidding now mainstream since COVID
final_text: On 29 June 2020 Oliver Barker, alone in a London studio, auctioned to phone banks in NY, Hong Kong and London; Bacon's Oresteia triptych made $84.6M after a 10-minute duel with an online bidder in China.
source_note: Sotheby's press release: livestreamed global sale, $363.2M

original: Third major house, founded 1796
final_text: Phillips was founded in London in 1796 by Harry Phillips, formerly a clerk to James Christie; with no staff or premises he held a dozen sales in year one, selling anything from tea services to a saddle mare.
source_note: Founder Christie's clerk; first-year sales, varied goods

original: Known for contemporary art, watches, design
final_text: On 26 Oct 2017 Phillips (with Bacs & Russo) sold Paul Newman's own Rolex Daytona, engraved 'DRIVE CAREFULLY ME' by Joanne Woodward, for $17,752,500 after 12 minutes, a wristwatch record.
source_note: Sale date, inscription, price, bidding duration

original: More youthful, edgier than Christie's/Sotheby's
final_text: Phillips was bought by Bernard Arnault's LVMH in 1999; after heavy losses it became Phillips, de Pury & Luxembourg in 2001, and Moscow's Mercury Group took a majority stake in October 2008.
source_note: Ownership chain LVMH, de Pury, Mercury Group

original: Consignment: owner gives work to auction house
final_text: Divorce feeds the rooms: after Harry and Linda Macklowe's bitter split, a court ordered their 65 works sold; Sotheby's auctioned them in Nov 2021 and May 2022 for $922.2 million.
source_note: Court-ordered Macklowe sale, two parts, $922M total

original: Estimate: low-high range published in catalogue
final_text: Estimates are opening gambits: Christie's put Salvator Mundi at about $100 million in 2017, and Sotheby's estimated Bacon's Oresteia triptych at $60-80 million before it made $84.6 million.
source_note: Salvator ~$100M estimate; Bacon estimate via Sotheby's coverage

original: Reserve: secret minimum price below which won't sell
final_text: The reserve is the confidential minimum agreed by consignor and house, never printed in the catalogue, and it cannot be set above the lot's low estimate.
source_note: Christie's glossary: reserve confidential, not above low estimate

original: Premium: buyer pays 25% on top of hammer price
final_text: The buyer's premium is tiered, not a flat 25%: from September 2025 Christie's charges 27% of hammer up to $1.5M, 22% from $1.5M to $8M, and 15% above $8M.
source_note: Grossman LLP summary of Christie's Sept 2025 tiers

original: Seller pays 10-25% commission to house
final_text: At the top, sellers often pay nothing: a coveted consignor may have the commission waived and even pocket part of the buyer's premium, a deal the trade calls an 'enhanced hammer'.
source_note: Enhanced hammer: fee waived, share of premium

original: "Chandelier bidding" - auctioneer pretends to see bids
final_text: Chandelier bidding is legal in New York only below the reserve: the auctioneer may bid for the seller up to that figure; NYC rules once required catalogues to disclose it, later repealed.
source_note: Center for Art Law: legal below reserve, NYC rules

original: "Bought in" = didn't meet reserve, unsold
final_text: A lot that fails to reach its reserve is 'bought in', and the trade calls it 'burned'; burned works usually resell later for less, often at a different house.
source_note: ArtTactic: burned works, lower resale, house switching

original: Provenance: ownership history (gaps are red flags)
final_text: Provenance haunts sales: Yasuda bought Van Gogh's Sunflowers at Christie's London on 30 March 1987 for £24.75M; in 2022 heirs of banker Paul von Mendelssohn-Bartholdy sued its owner Sompo, citing Nazi-era duress.
source_note: Art Newspaper: Sunflowers 1987 sale and heirs' lawsuit

original: Condition report: damage, restoration
final_text: Christie's published Salvator Mundi's condition report: by 1900 it had been 'grotesquely repainted', even given a beard; conservator Dianne Modestini removed overpaint and inpainted losses in 2007-10.
source_note: Art Newspaper on Christie's Salvator Mundi condition report

original: Literature: published references
final_text: The online Cezanne catalogue raisonne (Feilchenfeldt, Warman, Nash) lists 40+ literature references for Le Garcon au gilet rouge, and its lot no. 6 at Sotheby's on 15 Oct 1958; Paul Mellon bought it.
source_note: Catalogue raisonne entry: provenance, literature, Mellon

original: Exhibition history
final_text: Monet's Haystacks debuted at Durand-Ruel, Paris, on 4 May 1891, fifteen stacks among 22 new canvases; Bertha Palmer of Chicago bought nine. One Palmer 'Meules' made $110.7M at Sotheby's in May 2019.
source_note: Art Institute of Chicago; 2019 price via CBC report

original: Authentication letters
final_text: Authentication is perilous: the Andy Warhol Foundation dissolved its authentication board in early 2012 after spending nearly $7 million defending an antitrust suit over a rejected 1964 self-portrait.
source_note: Board dissolution, legal costs, Joe Simon lawsuit

original: Many top works never go to auction
final_text: Gauguin's Nafea Faa Ipoipo (1892) never went to auction: in 2015 the Staechelin family, who had lent it to the Kunstmuseum Basel, sold it privately to a Qatari buyer, reportedly for nearly $300 million.
source_note: Private sale per NYT; price reported, not confirmed

original: Discreet, no public price
final_text: In 2011 the estate of Greek shipowner George Embiricos, who never lent it out, sold a version of Cezanne's The Card Players privately to Qatar's royal family, reportedly for about $250 million.
source_note: Vanity Fair report summarised; price estimated, never disclosed

original: "Guaranteed price" deals with third parties
final_text: Third-party guarantees appear in catalogues as an 'irrevocable bid' symbol: an outside party has committed to bid at a level that ensures the lot sells.
source_note: Sotheby's lot-symbol guide: irrevocable bid ensures sale

original: Art advisors, intermediaries, secrecy
final_text: In 2013 Swiss dealer Yves Bouvier bought Salvator Mundi in a Sotheby's-brokered private deal for $80M and resold it within days to Dmitry Rybolovlev for $127.5M, sparking years of lawsuits.
source_note: artnet: Bouvier markup, Rybolovlev dispute

original: Collectors: old money, new money, oligarchs, tech billionaires
final_text: In May 1990 paper magnate Ryoei Saito bought Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr Gachet at Christie's for $82.5M and, two days later, Renoir's Bal du moulin de la Galette for $78.1M; he later joked of cremating them.
source_note: Saito purchases, prices, cremation remark later called joke

original: Dealers: galleries, private dealers, runners
final_text: With their dealer Durand-Ruel short of cash, Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Morisot auctioned 73 works at the Hotel Drouot on 24 March 1875; the crowd jeered, police were called, and the artists bought some back.
source_note: Drouot 1875 sale, riot, artists bought back works

original: Museums: often can't compete on price
final_text: Alan Bond bought Van Gogh's Irises at Sotheby's NY in Nov 1987 for $53.9M with Sotheby's lending him about half; unable to pay, he sold it in 1990 to the J. Paul Getty Museum for an undisclosed sum.
source_note: artnet: Bond, Sotheby's loan, Getty purchase 1990

original: Art advisors: paid by collectors to guide purchases
final_text: In January 2016 Sotheby's bought the advisory firm Art Agency, Partners of Amy Cappellazzo and Allan Schwartzman for up to $85 million, buying the advisers' client book.
source_note: Art Newspaper: $50M plus $35M earn-out deal
